title: What the Needle Kept
content:
Every night after the last bather left, Ines Karvat went down to the cellar and wound the drum her husband had installed the year the bathhouse opened, and every morning she changed its paper without looking at it. Teodor had told the town of Sulz that the drum took the temperature of the spring. On the eve of the frost feast, with two hundred tickets sold, the sheet tore as she lifted it and she looked: where she had always supposed a flat grey thread, the needle had drawn a comb. The bathhouse had its wras, like any building that age, and like any wras it had waited until there was no ear in the place; only the needle had been down there with it. Behind the spare rolls she found a surveyor's report dated a year before the foundations, with a fault inked in red straight through the hot pool and Teodor's initials beside the word *advised*. She took it upstairs to show him, or to burn it; she had not decided on the stairs.

In the changing room the long mirror was fogged, as always, and she wiped it with her sleeve, as always. The woman in the glass stood with her eyes shut and her hands out for a fresh sheet of paper, and Ines saw that this was how she had looked every morning for twelve years: like someone taking great care.

Teodor was at the boiler in his feast waistcoat, and he saw the red line before he saw her face. "Fire and paper," he said, swinging the firebox open for her. "Shortest marriage there is, and nobody's ever the worse for it." She asked how long he had known, and he said since before he knew her, as if that were a kindness. She shut the firebox with her foot and folded the report into her apron.

At six the doors opened and she stood on the top step and read it to the queue: the depth, the dates, the word *advised*. They listened the way people listen to grace; old Mrs. Oll patted her arm, the mayor said Teodor Karvat had built the only warm room in the valley, and then they went in past her, and paid. By seven the whole town was in the water with children on its shoulders, and Teodor moved along the edge with a tray of plum spirit, not looking toward the door.

Ines went down to the cellar, where the needle lay still, as it always did with people in the building, and found she no longer believed it. She put both hands on the sluice wheel he had told her never to touch in season and turned it until it stopped. Upstairs the singing thinned and broke off, and when she climbed back the town of Sulz was standing naked in a basin of wet tile, furious, looking for someone to blame and finding her. Teodor set down his tray. With the water gone, everyone could see the crack across the floor of the hot pool, thin as a line on paper, and in the quiet something small came up out of it, like one tooth being tried against another.
premise: Ines Karvat wants to keep her husband's bathhouse open for the frost feast, but the drum in the cellar has drawn the line he swore the ground would never draw.

title: Orad
content:
For nine days after the frost feast the crack in the drained pool talked, and for nine days Dr. Almut Reiss sat at the open window of her observatory above Sulz with her better ear turned toward the town. She had been blind two winters. The comet tables published under her name in that time were in Jonna Weil's hand, from Jonna's eye at the glass, and neither of them had ever said so aloud, which was why they no longer ate at the same table. Jonna's letter to the Academy lay on the desk, wanting only a signature. "Bring me what the stone says, stroke for stroke," said Dr. Reiss, "and I'll sign whatever you slide under my pen."

The bathhouse was roped off, and the only person who knew the way beneath it was Teodor Karvat, whom the town now crossed the street to avoid, and who said yes before she had finished asking. He took her down past the boiler, past a drum with a dry needle, into a culvert he had laid with his own hands. "It has a throat, and we're in it," he said. "Keep orad, and put your weight on nothing I haven't put mine on." They went orad forty yards on their bellies with the lantern pushed ahead, the rock sweating, the sound growing from a tick to a mutter to something with stops in it like speech. At the lip, where she could look up through the split floor of the pool and see feast lanterns still hanging in the rafters, she got out her pencil.

It was not words. She wrote what there was, long, long, short, a grind, a silence, and knew Dr. Reiss would run a thumb over the page and feel that it was nothing. Teodor lay with his cheek on the stone. "I've had twelve years of this on paper," he said. "I never once listened to it, but I can read."

He ared it for her with a finger on her page: that is the east side taking the weight, that is it slipping a hair, that silence is the hold before the next. The holds were getting shorter; she could count them herself, eleven breaths, then nine, then eight. "Tonight," he said. "Before light." He had told the whole town, in that same level voice, that the ground would never move.

If she rang the fire bell on his word and morning came whole, there would be no signature, no Academy, and no door in Sulz that would open to her. "Why would I believe you?" she said. "Don't," said Teodor. "Count." Six breaths. She left the page under the lantern and backed out of the throat faster than she had gone in, then crossed the square to the fire tower with her knees bleeding through her stockings. The rope was stiff with frost, so she hung her whole weight on it, and above her the bell turned over and spoke.
premise: Jonna Weil wants the blind astronomer's signature on her letter to the Academy, but the price is a transcript of what the cracked pool is saying, and the only guide to it is the man who built the bathhouse on the crack.

title: The King of the Baths
content: Nobody died in Sulz, because a girl rang a bell. What happened instead was that the spring got loose from its pipes and ran warm down every street for a month, and when it was fin
premise: Ines Karvat wants to leave on Thursday's coach with her one trunk, but every night her husband walks asleep into the stone town, and she is the only one he will turn for.
